tkamat29|root|parent|prev|next|

Why would you want to hone in on finding "good programmers" though? Programming is not the end-all be-all skill of being a good software engineer, this was true even before AI but is even more true now.

Leetcode is popular because:

1. It gauges problem solving ability and pattern recognition, which are essential to any job, and particularly useful for software engineers.

2. It is language agnostic - most jobs would rather have a strong engineer that doesn't know their particular language/tech stack than a weak engineer that is familiar with the stack.

3. It has objective evaluation criteria (correctness + time/space complexity).

It's certainly not perfect, but I have yet to see an alternative that accomplishes all of the above. The one thing I can see potentially complementing it is the new style of AI-assisted assessment where you are dropped into an unknown codebase, and asked to make fixes/features that are assisted by an AI agent. This solves the language-agnostic issue with pre-AI versions of these interviews, where you had to have memorized specific tech stack features or language syntax in order to accomplish the task. Now AI can take care of that stuff, and the interviewee can focus on the problem solving aspect.

Mawr|root|parent|prev|next|

> This is a classic fallacy: that interview should look the same as the job.

I think I'm gonna get a stroke reading this. The classic fallacy is the nonsense you're spouting — that there's anything besides the job itself that is relevant to it. You're hiring people for x, so the only thing you care about is their ability to do x. This is obvious.

The perfect test is just hiring someone on the spot and seeing how they perform. We don't do this because it's expensive but obviously it would be the perfect test, measuring exactly what you're hiring for, by definition.

So then any test that goes further and further away from that ideal becomes worse and worse at predicting job performance. The trick is figuring out a good enough test that's still reasonably quick and cheap to do.

Deliberately going out of your way to test your canditates for something unrelated to the job is insanely stupid.

It's essentially just arrogance. Arrogantly asserting that you know for sure your particular "generic" test actually selects for ~all traits you want while also rejecting ~all traits you don't. I assure you, the chances of you having a good enough model of reality to do this are laughable. Pure arrogance.

Again, easiest to see by thinking of the opposite example to before — the worst test possible would of course be something completely unrelated, so idk, having a chef play ping-pong. I'm sure you could convincingly argue it tests something, but why in the world would you not just have him make a dish, since you know, that's what you're hiring him to do? (it's not actually by the way, now that's a classic fallacy — that the job is the mechanical subset of it and not the job as a whole. Soft skills, anyone? sigh).

I've seen someone suggesting that since a lot of programmers like playing Factorio, why not interview people by having them play Factorio? Ah, because then you're selecting for Factorio players. Do you have a good model of what makes a good Factorio player? Hell, do you have a good model of what makes a good performer at your job? You absolutely do not. Why select for Factorio players when you can select for your-job players?

Another common example of this utter arrogance is thinking that a candidate's performance during a highly stressful, unnatural, and artificial classic interview grilling environment is indicative of their perfomance in the every day feeling-secure-in-their-job state of mind. Oh, look, this fool I'm basically abusing from my position of power is stammering and squirming, must mean he's a good-for-nothing loser! Hah, another fraud found!

So sure, keep putting people in as much stress as possible and asking them how many golf balls fit in an airplane. BTW, I walk out of such interviews immediately. Have fun with your new Leetcode grinder performative actor hires though — you get what you test for.

You're making a lot of assumptions about the owner that often don't really pan out. For example I have less than zero love for the Waltons but Walmart is just such a great example. Their gross profit margin is about 24%. That's how much they profit on each item sold. But then after you factor in their operating costs, labor in particular, it's down to 3%.

So the Walton's money printing button comes from taking 3 pennies from each dollar, but at a very high volume. If Walmart wanted to e.g. significantly raise the wages they pay, they'd have to substantially increase the prices on everything sold. The balance of higher wages for some but higher costs for all would almost certainly be a significant net-loss for the lower half of society.

And this issue is even more pervasive at smaller shops. Making ends meet is even harder for small business owners. The idea that somebody's just printing money because they own a business is unrealistic. Well it's kind of true for tech businesses, but I suspect we're going to see that change in the future - though that's another topic altogether.

That is what makes me more nervous, as what is playing out now in both the US and EU is a shift from monetary to fiscal dominance, with significant disruption of white collar occupations that has been predicted even within a world without modern generative AI.

So the question is if demand for software will expand by more than the productivity improvement it creates, in this fiscal environment. I think it will, but it will be for Software as a (Specific) Solution rather than the classic Software as a Service (delivering measurable outcomes vs. delivering tools for people to use), and this will come with a shift in the types of roles hired for. Less "routine" software developers, more people in product design, more domain specialists, more system architects and integration engineers, QA, security, compliance & auditing, etc...

lallysingh|root|parent|next|

My experience is exactly the opposite. 30 years writing software for my job, been using claude/grok for most of this year. At first they were really amazing. A real lever for higher output. But, I spend most of my time now telling them how to design high-performance systems and how to manage high concurrency and low contention.

They'll shove out a pattern quickly, but no matter how new and magical the latest model is, they will just put out some tweaked variant of existing designs. I find myself treating it like a junior-mid engineer. "Add rdtsc-based timers around major parts of the code to whittle down what's taking too long." "Use that to figure out where the transfer amount is way too small to justify the time taken without copying the payload." etc.

But concurrency bugs from large LLM-developed codebases are a major issue. They constantly find bugs they wrote. I eventually told it to start writing formal models of the concurrent uses and to (a) validate the models; (b) verify the code implements the models; to make it work.

So yeah, I stand by my words. For simple commands and tiny codebases, it /can/ do those things, but even small projects (50 KLOC) are a mess of making it fix its own mistakes, reconcile basic logic in requirements analysis, and everything has to be taken over with a fine-tooth comb to make it any good.

chrisco255|root|parent|prev|next|

You bring 27 years of experience and context to every single LLM session you open, so every session you have with an LLM is already going to be far more productive than someone starting from scratch with zero experience in application development. You're able to understand how to map business requirements to technical outcomes and you can competently direct the LLMs to the desired outcome. That is the high-value part of your job that has always existed. It never was about coding the solution in whatever esoteric Turing-complete language you used.

As for legacy software suddenly failing us, what you're really talking about are active systems like Microsoft 365 (it's not legacy code). Those systems have always been complex. That they are "suddenly" failing could be an indication of a number of things, but I'd pin a large part of the responsibility on organizational debt (even beyond technical debt). Maintaining complex software systems is hard, software mostly isn't a static thing it has to constantly evolve. It could also be an indication of over-reliance on LLM competency, for all we know about those system's internals. We just don't know enough to make an assessment.

There have been some zero days discovered by LLMs. There have also been many socially engineered, regular old exploits that have been impressed on us as indications of AI breakouts.

As for speedups, most software is comically unoptimized and has been for some time. We made an explicit trade-off in software development as CPUs and machines got more capable: we started coding in simpler languages with higher levels of abstraction (Python, Ruby, JS, Java, etc) sometimes costing us 10x or more in resource utilization, in exchange for the iteration speed that bought us. Converting those to more efficient languages like Go, Rust, C, etc alone buys you so much. On top of that, there are a number of algorithmic optimizations most developers never implemented that map to well known access patterns in hardware. Lots of low hanging fruit.

matheusmoreira|root|parent|prev|next|

It's as scns said: the sense of achievement is gone.

I once reverse engineered my laptop's keyboard LEDs and made Linux free software to control them. Other people inexplicably found my project and built on top of it. I was really proud of that.

Then I subscribed to frontier LLMs and they made short work of that same laptop's entire firwmare blob in about a day. Solved some long standing mysteries. And I felt literally nothing.

This is one reason, but not the only reason.

I've been hobby programming alone for over a decade. When I finally subscribed to frontier AIs, it was like a shot in the arm. I finally had a coding buddy, someone to talk to about my projects, who would review and criticize my code. I learned so much I had to pause and let it sink in so I could understand what I was doing.

But the hobbyist niche I wanted to be part of turned out to be thoroughly hostile to LLMs and their users. I went from a guy who was interviewed in Lobsters for his programming language work to a guy whose work turned into slop essentially overnight, and the rift only grew wider over time.

So the sense of accomplishment is gone and now people whose respect I wanted call my work slop because LLMs touched it. This left me in this weird emotional state where I feel guilty for using AIs at all but know that it's impossible to go back to how things were before. It's been months since I've touched my open source projects. I just can't find the will to do it. I'm working on private stuff now, hopefully things that will make me some amount of money in the future.

There's also the fact that AIs are changing society so thoroughly that governments are becoming extremely intolerant of personal computing and the subversive freedom it affords all of us. There is constant talk of AI regulation, and dystopian technology like remote hardware attestation is already becoming mandatory. We're also being literally priced out of computers.

So it's becoming literally pointless. What is the point of free software if we can't run it? If running it gets us ostracized from digital society? If it makes us criminals? If we can't even afford computers in the first place? To me it looks like everything the free software community worked so hard for will have been in vain.

brightball|root|parent|next|

There were a lot of reasons for it.

Java itself was a much slower standard workflow. Dynamic languages in general, like Ruby, Python, Perl or PHP were much faster to work with than the burdensome recompile workflows. Think instant feedback vs waiting for your CI to finish after every single save. The speed of iteration was critical.

Beyond that, when the speed of development is slower, more people get hired to do the work. When more people get hired to do the work, there's more communication relay as the team size grows. Teams coordinating between each other. Decisions going to committees. Middle management layers.

You'd routinely see companies with 3-5 Rails devs outperforming shops with 50 Java devs. Communication and iteration speed was huge. The other piece of it was the convention over configuration aspect because it removed so many things you'd have to discuss and make decisions about as a group which further accelerated communications.

10-20x multiplier isn't an exaggeration at all. If anything I could be underselling it.


buu700|root|parent|prev|next|

I see both types of claims a lot on HN, and find both credible.

On one extreme, a solo dev could prompt a frontier SOTA agent with not much more than "Build Uber", give it the necessary hardware/software/permissions to build itself a useful feedback loop and act autonomously, put it in goal mode, and let it cook, and as long as the tokens kept flowing they'd eventually end up with something reasonable in actual orders of magnitude less time than it would have taken that dev to build the same thing — especially if you're counting calendar days rather than hours worked, and extra especially if they wouldn't have had the luxury of investing full-time hours into that particular thing. At the opposite extreme, BigCo full-time SWE #5000 tasked with an extremely specific ticket for a critical revenue-generating brownfield system might experience even "20%" as liberal, and correctly observe that writing code was never the bottleneck for their job. And then there's the massive spectrum of circumstances in between those two ends.

None of that means that the gains aren't real, or that anyone in particular is wildly exaggerating in either direction. It just means the gains aren't evenly distributed.

kannanvijayan|root|parent|next|

I'm similarly working on a complex project and have run into these issues.

There's typically a combination of issues that are occurring when the codebase goes off the rails.

One is that cruft builds up. Large vibecoded codebases need regular "review cleaning". Where you review the whole thing top down for hygiene, contradictions, bad comments, style, redundancy, design. It's a standard thing for me now. A full review and cleanup pass once every couple months.

The second thing that tends to go wrong is that after a certain complexity threshold, the models cannot keep track of the relevant details for a task very well. They lose sense of project directionality. Every task gets disconnected from other tasks and they start pulling the system apart at the seams, exacerbating the cruft issue above and accelerating collapse.

I've found that separating my documentation into three distinct lobes helps: goaling docs, guardrail docs, and implementation docs. Goaling docs describe in prose the goals of the project which includes scope, certain design targets, and other things that you are aiming towards. Guardrails are for design and implementation choices you have explicitly ruled out, the "what not to do" part. Impl docs describe the state of the system as it is.

The top-level agent documents refer to these and make their purpose explicit.

You'd think a ticketing system might capture this, but it doesn't really provide the richness of expression a collection of documents in a directory does.

These approaches aren't perfect. The process still has a tendency to wander off the rails, but it happens less often now and I catch it more quickly. Every session misses little bits of the goaling alignment, but they also find and address small issues missed by previous sessions. Overall it does a better job of keeping the codebase hovering around some threshold of coherency.

I'm having a lot of fun to be honest. Yes it's bizarre and nothing like what development used to be, but it finally feels like there's some new things to learn now.

Take this as genuine advice, not criticism: The fact that you felt the need to “characterize” the jank and verbally describe it is evidence of your mistake. The only way for these new development models to function is to create a tight machine-only validation loop. Every aspect of an LLM-generated text editor must be drivable fully by the LLM itself so that it can independently observe the problems and fix them (and so those observations can be mechanically translated to regression test cases)

LLMs won’t always guide you to do this correctly so you need to understand how important it is from the start and always enforce it.

semiquaver|root|parent|next|

Then the equivalence I refer to is not in place.

The software’s behavior that a human can observe must be observable by the agent. Any interaction the human can perform should also be performable by the agent.

microtonal|root|parent|prev|next|

Our work will change, we will spend less time on tedium, we will become more ambitious. Barring an architectural paradigm shift we will still need people with strong engineering and design instincts, and even more importantly the ability to write reference code and formal specifications codifying desired behaviors.

It is hard to say how things will develop the coming years, but this sums it up for me today. Almost constantly, LLMs (e.g. Opus 5.5/Sonnet 5.5) make choices that a junior programmer would think is ok, but I know that will create technical debt, subpar designs, etc. Note that I'm not saying that LLMs program like a junior programmer, in many ways they program like senior engineers who have happened to memoize all API docs as well. But they are often missing the larger context or don't understand the time dimension (what will be hard to maintain, what will introduce an API that we can not easily backtrack from, etc). So, I am not surprised that vibecoding breaks down as a project becomes larger.

At the same time, current LLMs make me a lot more productive (which was not true for me ~one year ago). I can do in 30-60 minutes what would take me a day 1-2 years ago. In many ways, programming also became more interesting, because I can focus on design, the really challenging parts, while the LLM can quickly implement it. LLMs really feel like a different, in many ways complementary intelligence for development.

I ran into a similar issue with Gemini 3.8 in an even simpler context. Spent several hours asking it why my new module wasn't working and each time after several minutes of thinking it would exclaim "I FOUND THE ROOT CAUSE!" and despite implementing its fix the problem would still persist.

After about a dozen failed iterations I reverted to the last known working commit (albeit with the new module only partially implemented), isolated the issue as best I could, then asked Gemini again and this time it correctly identified a latent timing bug that was the cause of all the problems.

In short, I had to manually reduce the complexity of the problem for this magic infinity-dimensional-processor to deduce what the problem was. Maybe it would have gotten there eventually, but without AI I would have just reverted the commit a lot sooner and likely figured it out on my own with some basic debug logging.

Programming is going the way of skilled trades. And that's okay.

Think of electricians, plumbers, carpenters, mechanics, etc. People can and do attempt and often complete that work themselves, but larger projects, professional projects, and people that don't have the time nor expertise but want a good job done pay professionals to do the work. The AI is the toolset, and experience in using the tool and knowing where and how it works best and the tricks to make it work effectively will be the real distinction, between a layman and professional.

There will also be people that are more specifically on the software engineering side, where they might be equivalent to a contractor or an architect depending on size and complexity and how much is design and how much is assembly, so it won't just be people assembling stuff from AI designs.

All that's happening is that we'll get some stratification of roles by what different positions are good at, and we might get some actual certifications that mean something, and while the total number of professional programmers might go down, there will still be a need for them at all skill levels, and the general public will dabble in it much more often.

There's going to be a shake up and a rough time for surplus programmers, but just as there was a surplus of woodworkers that had hard times when the assembly line was introduced and popularized, it will normalize over time. I suggest people either lean into their tooling a lot to learn how to use it well enough to be those that survive that culling, or look into related fields that won't be eaten quite as much which they can inch towards.

Note: If you are in a growth industry or company, you'll be safer than if you aren't as lack of need to hire or slowed hiring may be the local result instead. So staying if you're in those or finding those may also be a good strategy for a while.

It is not silly to compare them, but the comparison is not very favourable to Anthropic once you put the two sums in context.

Anthropic will burn through the amount of money they raised (by selling between 5 and 7.5% of the company) in twelve months — on their immediate commitments for next year ($70B or so) and their projected losses for Q4 2026 alone (over $12B).

They are loss-making, and while they have a pretty pile of investor cash, they have hundreds of billions of dollars of future commitments; their commitments until 2030 are about three times the size of it, I think, even if you add in what they just raised?

Add to that: it's not really clear that their only product lines make them money unless you exclude the cost of training them.

Google was profitable at IPO and had been for at least the previous year, the IPO floated a similar share of the company (7.23% apparently) but raised more than 3.5 times their yearly operating costs, or roughly about three times their total outstanding commitments at that point, according to their S-1.

Google was in a healthy position, and basically put the cash in the kitty to use for future projects.

Anthropic is in a historically huge debt and obligation hole. It has sold off a chunk of the business so they can run just to stand still, and its problems get worse after the next year, while its cost and difficulty of raising debt is likely to increase (unless JP Morgan and Goldman Sachs somehow convince the ratings agencies to give them a non-junk credit rating).

My top priority today is raising my kids, which LLMs have been stupendously unhelpful with, although they were pretty useful in setting up a home server and Jellyfin so I could give them a curated, parent-vetted set of TV shows to watch.

But AI is terrible at doing anything unique, personalized, and based on your own desires, because it doesn't have your desires. It's building on a corpus of shared knowledge, but there is a large set of knowledge that is unshared, and it can't do anything for that. A large portion of business, for example, is secrets and lies, and an LLM isn't going to be able to help you much with that. At its best it can set up the frameworks and tools to help you keep secrets and tell lies.

And then a large portion of life is personal preferences, the things that make you unique and distinct from every other human, and an LLM can't help you with that either. There is a reason I don't have a nanny raise my kids, even though we could afford it. If I did that, it would be the nanny raising my kids, which defeats a lot of the point of having kids in the first place. LLMs have the same problem.

beachy|root|parent|next|

The specific area was airline control systems. I'm well out of anything to do with that now, but a long time ago these systems were absolutely engineered for performance and so C was radical as a high level language that could compete with pure assembler for speed.

Two examples of the lengths people went to for performance - 1) the networking hardware, terminals and everything were special airline flavors that sent data in 6 bits rather than 8, just to squeeze more data onto the wire. Is you look over someone's shoulder at an airline booking screen even now you'll see an all caps look - that's why. All caps means less bits.

The second was a little before my time but the geniuses who maintained the assembler code were very close to the hardware. Some used programming tricks to account for the rotational speed of the DASD, so the software would be ready to pull bits off the hard drive just as those bits rotated around and arrived at the read heads. Insane optimisations.

I'm out of the area now so I didn't know what the state of the art is, presumably there's not any IBM assembler still lurking but it certainly wouldn't surprise me.

beachy|root|parent|next|

Think 6 bit frames instead of 8. All the way through the hardware and software and network stack. Special networking hardware variants specifically built to use 6 bit bytes.

ijidak|parent|prev|next|

Yeah the interesting question regarding Anthropic is: do they build a software moat around their models?

Most of us, even myself, focus on the reality that models are likely to become a commodity and that means the big providers will be unable to maintain profitability off of their weights alone (ignoring whether or not they serve the infrastructure).

But what I have to give Anthropic credit for is that they bring to market products that work well enough incredibly fast and in that sense they remind me of Microsoft in the early '90s.

I use both Anthropic and OpenAI products and OpenAI products are so bad. Just incredibly clunky changing in strange and unnecessary ways. While problems that they should have fixed months ago, years ago, are still unfixed. No matter how fast you can build, you still have to build the right things.

It reminds me of a quote from Napoleon, which may be apocryphal and that I will likely butcher.

It was something along the lines of how Napoleon staffs his military. You have people that are smart and lazy, people that are smart and hardworking. You have people that are dumb and lazy and you have people that are dumb and hardworking.

He makes the lazy-and-smart generals, because they come up with good strategy but they're not excessively aggressive.

He makes the dumb and hardworking captains because they'll follow orders and lead their men.

He makes the dumb and lazy foot soldiers because they follow orders and they can be driven.

But the dumb and hardworking, he shoots because they both don't know what they're doing and they do a lot of it.

And I kind of feel that way regarding AI. AI makes everyone "hardworking." Now, with AI, everyone can get a lot of stuff done. But when it comes to product, if you're "dumb" regarding what to get done, you just do a lot of damage instead of producing results.

And between OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic... and I guess Meta.. Anthropic seems to be the only one of the big model providers that is both smart and "hardworking" (let's replace "hardworking" with "productive.").

Anthropic has a higher batting average on a lot of their productization ideas and does so quickly.

And ultimately that might be Anthropic's moat -- just as Apple's moat in smartphones was not that no one else could make a similar smartphone, but that no one else executed as well end-to-end for the customer during the Jobs era.

Even Anthropic's ability to get to an IPO before OpenAI is another example of them just doing things better.

It could be that this generation's Netscape is OpenAI and ChatGPT. While Anthropic ends up being this generation's early -90's Microsoft.

tristanj|root|parent|next|

Because stocks are valued on the discounted value of expected future earnings. The P/E ratio looks at the price compared to current earnings, specifically earnings over a trailing twelve-month period, which does not reflect expected future earnings.

In short, stocks are valued based on expected future performance. The P/E ratio reflects past performance.

Could someone explain how a company with a revenue of close to $17 billion per quarter gets a $2T valuation?

ion_trapper|parent|next|

The valuation of a company is what the last purchaser of its stock agreed to pay for it. There is no simple accounting formula that takes revenue and outputs that number. It is strictly a measure of what the last buyer thought the company was worth. That buyer may have used revenue in their calculations of worth, or maybe not. Maybe it was expectation of future revenue growth. Maybe they just liked the name.

This sounds arbitrary until you appreciate that the ones with most purchasing power on the market are also the same ones who have previously proven themselves to be capable asset allocators, as proven by their ability to accumulate capital. So the valuation of a company is not just every random Joe’s opinion equally averaged, but weighted towards those whose opinions on value have previously tended toward being correct (this includes capital acquired by any means, not just equity trading. For example, if you earned a lot of money with your own product, you have proven yourself to be able to judge value and effectively allocate resources too).

The market starts to make a lot more sense when you start to use it as an oracle of hidden information (“what is the market telling me about the value of X?”) instead of an irrational adversary (“why is the price Y? That doesn’t make sense!”).
